# How AI tooling was used

The brief permits AI tools and asks for the prompts I used along with my thinking. This
is an accurate record of both, including the parts that are not flattering. I have kept
it honest in preference to keeping it impressive, because the alternative is a document
that falls apart under one question in the interview.

**Tool:** Claude (Anthropic), run as an agentic coding session with read/write access to
the repository and a sandboxed shell.

**The short version:** this codebase was generated by the model from a single instruction
plus four scoping choices that I made. I did not dictate the domain model, the
idempotency strategy or the test design — the model proposed all of those. I overruled it
twice, and both are written up below: how money is handled, after a failing test exposed a
real bug, and where the order reference comes from, where I went against the model's
recommendation on a product question. Everything else here sets out where the line falls.

---

## The prompts, verbatim

There were two pieces of input from me. Both are reproduced in full.

### 1. The opening instruction

> Please help me to complete the attached assessment based on the below instructions and
> guide me on how best i can record the video and what i can cover/include to increase my
> chances of getting an interview:

...followed by the assignment PDF and the full text of the invitation email.

### 2. Four scoping decisions

The model stopped before writing any code and asked me to choose. These are the questions
it put to me and the answers I gave:

| Question | My answer |
| --- | --- |
| How ambitious should the backend architecture be? | **Clean-ish layered** — Api / Application / Domain / Infrastructure, rich domain model, repository abstraction. Over a single project with folders, or full DDD + CQRS + MediatR. |
| How should the app store orders? | **EF Core InMemory by default, SQLite as a configurable option** — over a plain thread-safe in-memory repository or a JSON file. |
| Which extras should I include? | **All four** — status changes and filtering in the UI, a concurrency test for duplicates, Swagger with ProblemDetails errors, Docker Compose and CI. |
| Do you have the .NET 8 SDK and Angular CLI installed? | Not sure, needed to check. |

That is the entire set of instructions behind this repository.

---

## What I decided, and what the model decided

**Mine.** The four choices above are real decisions and I will defend them. The layered
structure over CQRS was a judgement that MediatR pipelines on a four-hour internal CRUD
app read as ceremony rather than seniority, and that the reviewer would rather hear me
justify a boundary than count abstractions. EF Core over a `ConcurrentDictionary` was so
the duplicate guard could be a real database constraint rather than a lock I had written
myself, which makes it a claim about production behaviour instead of a demo. Taking all
four extras was a deliberate trade of polish for surface area, on the reasoning that the
video is scored on the depth of the reasoning I can show and each extra is another
decision worth narrating.

**The model's.** Everything else, and it is a long list: the `Order` aggregate with a
private line collection and a static factory; using the client's external reference as an
idempotency key scoped to the customer; the SHA-256 request fingerprint that separates a
true replay from a reference reused with different contents; which fields are material to
that fingerprint and which are cosmetic; the three-layer concurrency defence and the
admission that the in-process gate is worthless across instances; the status transition
policy and the decision to treat a repeated status as a silent success; RFC 7807 error
shapes; the entire Angular application; and the first drafts of the README and
SOLUTION.md.

I am not going to dress those up as mine. They are good decisions and I agree with them,
but agreeing with a decision after the fact is not the same as having made it, and the
interview will find the difference.

---

## Overrule 1: money

The first of the two decisions that changed because I disagreed with the generated answer,
and the more technical one, so it is worth setting out properly.

I ran `dotnet test`. Three tests failed, all in `OrderTotalsTests`, all on the same
theory: a line of 3 × 0.005 was expected to total 0.02 and produced 0.03. The model had
written the test and the implementation and they contradicted each other.

The cause was in `OrderLine`:

```csharp
UnitPrice = Money.Round(unitPrice);        // 0.005 -> 0.01
LineTotal = Money.Round(UnitPrice * qty);  // 0.01 * 3 = 0.03, not 0.015 -> 0.02
```

Rounding the *unit* price and then multiplying. On the failing test that is a cent. On a
realistic order it is not: three units at 9.995 are stored at 10.00 each and billed at
30.00 against a quoted 29.99, and the gap grows with the quantity. The stored price also
stops matching the price the rep typed, so nobody can reconcile it afterwards.

The obvious fix is to multiply first and round once. I did not do that, and the reason is
the part I would want to be asked about. The request validator was *already* rejecting
prices finer than a cent, so the domain was quietly rounding an input the API had promised
to refuse, and the failing test was feeding it values no real client could send. Three
components disagreeing about the same rule.

So the fix was to pick one answer and apply it in all three places: **a price finer than a
cent is refused, not rounded.** `Money.IsCentPrecision` is now the single definition, the
validator and the `OrderLine` constructor both call it, and the unit price is stored
exactly as submitted. A price we were not asked to change is not ours to change.

Two consequences I then had to be honest about rather than paper over:

- Line totals and the subtotal are now *exact* — cent prices times whole quantities. The
  SOLUTION.md claim that the subtotal is "the sum of already-rounded line totals" was no
  longer true and I rewrote it.
- `Money.Round` therefore never fires on the order path at all. The away-from-zero
  rounding mode is real and deliberate, but it is currently a guard for the first discount
  or tax rate rather than live behaviour. I moved its tests out of `OrderTotalsTests`,
  where they were implying otherwise, into a `MoneyTests` file that says so explicitly.

The generalisable lesson, and the one I would give in the interview: the model produced
code and tests that agreed with *each other* often enough that the suite passing would
have told me very little. What found this was running it and reading a failure properly
instead of making it green.

---

## Overrule 2: where the reference comes from

The second one is not a bug. It is a product decision, and the model argued against it.

I asked for the reference field to be auto-generated and disabled, because a rep typing
their own PO number is how you get the duplicates the system *cannot* catch: `PO-1001` and
`PO 1001` are different strings and the idempotency check is right to treat them as
different orders. The model pushed back with a real consequence — disabling the field
removes the UI's only route to the 409 conflict — and recommended an "unlock to override"
toggle so the conflict stayed reachable.

I declined the toggle. A control that exists so a demo can reach an error state is a
control a rep will eventually find and use, and then the field is back to being typed by
hand with extra steps. The conflict response exists for integrations, not for someone with
a keyboard, and it is fully covered by tests and reproducible through Swagger. I also
chose a sequential format over the date-plus-random one the model suggested, because a
reference a human has to read aloud on a phone call should be short and ordered.

Two things came out of that which are worth recording. The model was right about the
consequence and wrong about the remedy — flagging the cost was the useful contribution,
not the proposed fix. And I caught a follow-on effect neither of us had thought through:
once the form issues a fresh reference on every visit, the existing "Submit again" button
could no longer repeat anything, because a second visit is a genuinely new order. The
replay demo had to move to the order detail page, which is the only screen that still
knows a reference that has already been used. That is the kind of thing that only shows up
when you click through the change rather than reading the diff.

---

## Where the model was wrong

The money bug above is the most substantive one and it was found by running the tests.
These four are smaller and were found earlier, in a review pass the model ran over its own
output. Worth recording, because the useful lesson from this exercise is about failure
modes rather than about throughput:

- **A missing package reference.** `OrderIntake.Infrastructure` called
  `ConfigurationBinder.Get<T>()` without referencing
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder`. The API project inherits it from the
  ASP.NET Core shared framework, so the code looks fine in isolation; a plain class
  library has to ask for it. Straightforward compile error.
- **An HTTP status code that does not exist.** The error handler referenced
  `StatusCodes.Status499ClientClosedRequest`. 499 is nginx's convention, not an IANA code,
  so ASP.NET Core does not define a constant for it. Also a compile error.
- **A derived property about to be persisted.** `Order.AllowedTransitions` is computed
  from the status policy, but EF Core 8 maps primitive collections by convention and would
  have silently stored a copy of it, which then goes stale. Now explicitly ignored.
- **A nullability gap** in the notes validator under warnings-as-errors.

Two of those four would have stopped the build. This is the part I would emphasise if
asked what I learned: generated code that reads as entirely plausible can still fail to
compile, and the review pass is not optional overhead — it is where the actual engineering
happened.

A limitation worth stating rather than hiding: the environment the model ran in had no
access to the NuGet registry, so **the backend was never compiled or executed there.**
What that environment could verify was narrower — the dependency-free Domain project
compiles clean in Release with warnings-as-errors, every C# file parses cleanly under
C# 12 via the Roslyn parser, and the Angular application builds green under
`strictTemplates`. Everything else was a line-by-line reading. The first real build and
test run happened on my own machine, which is where the money bug surfaced; a review pass
that cannot execute anything was never going to find it.

The first build on my machine also failed, for an unrelated reason worth a line: my global
NuGet configuration includes a private Azure DevOps feed, and NuGet queries every
configured source for every package, so restore died on 401s against a feed that has
nothing to do with this project. The repository now pins its own `NuGet.config` with
`<clear />` on the package sources. That is a reproducibility fix rather than a workaround
— it means the repo restores identically on a reviewer's machine regardless of what their
own configuration says.

---

## My assessment of working this way

The honest finding is that the leverage is real and the exposure is real, and they scale
together. One instruction and four choices produced a working, layered, tested
application in a fraction of the time it would have taken me to type it. It also produced
a body of code whose design rationale lived entirely in the model until I sat down and
read it, and a first draft of this very document that invented a detailed collaboration
that had never taken place — which is a good illustration of the failure mode, since that
draft was fluent, specific and completely wrong.

What I would do differently is intervene earlier and more often. The points where a human
judgement genuinely changes the outcome are ahead of the code, not behind it: what
"duplicate" means to a sales rep, whether a corrected resubmission should be a conflict or
a silent overwrite, how much a four-hour brief should carry. I let most of those be
answered for me and then agreed with the answers. Reviewing a decision is cheaper than
making one, and it is not the same skill.

The two overrules are the counter-examples, and they are the reason I am reasonably
confident about the rest. The money one was only available to me because I ran the thing
and read a failure instead of making it green. The reference one came from the other
direction — the model flagged a real cost and proposed a remedy I did not want, and
deciding against it was a product judgement no amount of generated code was going to make
for me. That is the shape of the working relationship I would actually recommend: let the
model carry the volume, and spend your own attention on the two places it cannot reach —
where the code and its tests can agree with each other and still both be wrong, and where
the question is not what is correct but what the business wants.
